BREAKING: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -3.2 million barrels last week, to 276.4 million barrels, its lowest level since August 1982.

This follows declines of -2.65 million barrels and -399,000 barrels in the previous two weeks.

Since the March high, US SPR inventories have collapsed -139.1 million barrels, or -34%, down in 33 of the last 34 weeks.

The SPR now stands -450.3 million barrels, or -62%, below its all-time high set in 2010.

This is also just 5.9 million barrels above its lowest level on record, set in the week ending August 20th, 1982.

US oil reserves have rarely been this low.

A 40% re-rating of the Mag 7 amid solid breath for the broad market could lift both the cap- and equal-weight indices and breathe new life into both the cyclical and secular bull market. The chart below shows where we are in relation to the 150-year central trend, the 17-year secular bull market, and the 4-year cyclical bull market. 🧵(2/2)

I’m starting to take a more constructive view of the Mag 7 (or at least most of them). If the capex boom ends up slowing down for political or financial reasons, the Mag 7 may need to spend less of their cashflows on data center capex and more on share buybacks. If so, the payout ratio (dividends plus buybacks as a percent of earnings) could get a boost and that could lead to a re-rating of the group.  We can see below that the P/E ratio has been significantly derated, which in my view is the result of the steep decline in the payout ratio (from 63% last year to 29% currently). If the payout ratio were to move back up to its 2024-2025 average of 60%, my math suggests that the M7’s trailing P/E ratio could re-rate from 27x to 38x. In last week’s report I had suggested that the P/E multiple might double based on where the price/payout ratio is trading, but upon further reflection that seems too ambitious. A “meeting in the middle” seems more likely, with the P/PO ratio falling and the P/E ratio rising. 🧵(1/2)

BREAKING: Japan's exports jumped +20.5% YoY in October, to a record $74 billion, the 2nd-largest monthly increase since October 2022.

Japan’s exports have now grown for 14 consecutive months, the longest streak since 2021-2023.

The surge was led by semiconductor manufacturing equipment shipments, which soared +49.7% YoY.

This was followed by electrical machinery exports, at +33.6% YoY growth, reflecting strong global investment in AI infrastructure.

Among regions, exports to Taiwan led with +42.7% YoY growth, followed by ASEAN at +34.7%, the US at +23.9%, the EU at +22.1%, and China at +13.3%.

Global chip demand is transforming the Japanese economy.

BREAKING: Global fund managers cut their technology exposure by -25 percentage points in early November, to a net 12%, their biggest monthly decline since June 2006.

This marks even a larger monthly decline than during the 2022 bear market or the 2008 Financial Crisis.

As a result, technology is no longer the most overweight sector among fund managers.

The largest overweight positions are currently in Pharmaceuticals, at 34%, and Industrials, at 19%.

A record 38% of surveyed institutional investors believe companies are overinvesting, up from ~20% in January.

At the same time, 52% expect Big Tech companies to announce CapEx reductions over the next 6 months, up from 30% in October.

Institutional investors are rotating out of technology stocks at a rapid pace.
